claim: Tn5 transposase belongs to the retroviral integrase superfamily.
source: bioinformatic analysis and structural studies reveal that it belongs to the retroviral integrase superfamily that act on not only dsDNA but also RNA/DNA hybrids (for instance, RNase H).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on structural and bioinformatic analysis

claim: Proteins in the retroviral integrase superfamily share a conserved catalytic RNase H-like domain.
source: Despite the distinct substrates, these proteins all share a conserved catalytic RNase H-like domain (Figure 1a; Yang and Steitz, 1995; Savilahti et al., 1995; Nowotny, 2009; Rice and Baker, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1a showing structural comparison

claim: Tn5 transposase possesses in vitro tagmentation activity towards both strands of RNA/DNA hybrids.
source: In this study, we tested this hypothesis and found that indeed Tn5 possesses in vitro tagmentation activity towards both strands of RNA/DNA hybrids.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The Tn5 transposome sample exhibited a smear signal corresponding to small fragments ranging from ~30–650 base-pair (bp) after tagmentation of RNA/DNA hybrids.
source: Comparing with the heat-inactivated Tn5 sample or the blank control sample, the Tn5 transposome sample exhibited a modest but clear smear signal corresponding to small fragments ranging from ~30–650 base-pair (bp) (the blue patches in Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by Fragment Analyzer data shown in Figure 1c

claim: A down shift of large fragments ranging from ~700–4000 bp was observed after Tn5 tagmentation of RNA/DNA hybrids.
source: Consistent with the fragmentation event, we also observed a down shift of large fragments ranging from ~700–4000 bp (the orange patches in Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by Fragment Analyzer data shown in Figure 1c

claim: The fragmentation efficiency of RNA/DNA hybrids increased in a dose-dependent manner with the transposome.
source: In addition, the fragmentation efficiency increased in a dose-dependent manner with the transposome, suggesting that fragmentation of RNA/DNA hybrids is dependent on Tn5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b

claim: The Ct value of the Tn5 transposome sample is about eight cycles smaller than the heat inactivated Tn5 sample or the control sample.
source: We observed that cycle threshold (Ct) value of the Tn5 transposome sample is about eight cycles smaller than the heat inactivated Tn5 sample or the control sample, indicating approximately 256 times more amplifiable products (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1d

claim: Tn5 tagmentation produces approximately 256 times more amplifiable products from RNA/DNA hybrids compared to controls.
source: We observed that cycle threshold (Ct) value of the Tn5 transposome sample is about eight cycles smaller than the heat inactivated Tn5 sample or the control sample, indicating approximately 256 times more amplifiable products (Figure 1d).
evidence: Inferred from the 8-cycle difference in qPCR Ct values

claim: The performance of Tn5 remained similar across different buffer conditions.
source: We also tested different buffer conditions and found that the performance of Tn5 remained similar, indicating the robustness of the Tn5 tagmentation activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data across different buffer conditions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c

claim: Adaptor sequences are ligated to insert sequences during Tn5 tagmentation of RNA/DNA hybrids.
source: Using Sanger sequencing, we validated that the adaptor sequences are indeed ligated to the insert sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d

claim: The efficiency of Tn5 toward RNA/DNA hybrids is about 1/16 of that of dsDNA.
source: Average Ct value of the hybrids samples was about four cycles more than gDNA samples, indicating the efficiency of Tn5 toward hybrids is about 1/16 of that of dsDNA (Figure 1e).
evidence: Inferred from 4-cycle difference in qPCR Ct values between hybrids and dsDNA

claim: Natural RNA/DNA hybrids favor A-form conformation.
source: It is known that natural RNA/DNA hybrids favor A-form conformation.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: In the presence of PEG200, RNA/DNA hybrids favor B-form conformation.
source: Interestingly, in the presence of PEG200, hybrids were found to favor B-form conformation (Pramanik et al., 2011), which we expected to make the hybrids a better substrate of Tn5.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pramanik et al., 2011

claim: Addition of PEG200 greatly improves the Tn5 tagmentation efficiency towards RNA/DNA hybrids.
source: Indeed, addition of PEG200 diminishes this difference by greatly improving the Tn5 tagmentation efficiency towards hybrids (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing conditions with and without PEG200 shown in Figure 1e

claim: The conformation of substrates affects the preference of Tn5.
source: This result indicates that the conformation of substrates certainly affects the preference of Tn5.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PEG200 (which changes conformation) improves tagmentation efficiency

claim: An 8-cycle difference between Tn5 transposome sample (Ct = 22.68) and the control sample (Ct = 30.40) was reproducibly observed for annealed RNA/DNA hybrids.
source: A 8-cycle difference between Tn5 transposome sample (Ct = 22.68) and the control sample (Ct = 30.40) was reproducibly observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h

claim: Tn5 has a direct tagmentation activity towards RNA/DNA hybrids.
source: While it is unclear this difference in tagmentation efficiency obtained from short oligos can be applied to long oligos, this result clearly demonstrates that Tn5 has a direct tagmentation activity towards RNA/DNA hybrids.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from annealed RNA/DNA hybrids where no dsDNA is possible

claim: RNA/DNA duplexes can be found in R-loop and chromatin-bound lncRNAs in vivo.
source: RNA/DNA duplexes can be found in many in vivo scenarios, including but not limited to R-loop and chromatin-bound lncRNAs (Santos-Pereira and Aguilera, 2015; Li and Fu, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Traditional RNA-seq library construction involves many laborious and time-consuming steps, including mRNA purification, fragmentation, reverse transcription, second-strand synthesis, end-repair and adaptor ligation.
source: Because traditional RNA-seq library construction involves many laborious and time-consuming steps, including mRNA purification, fragmentation, reverse transcription, second-strand synthesis, end-repair and adaptor ligation, we attempted to replace the process using the tagmentation activity towards RNA/DNA duplexes.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about traditional RNA-seq methods

claim: TRACE-seq uses total RNA as input material.
source: With the help of TRACE-seq, these steps are replaced with a 'one-tube' protocol (Figure 2a), which uses total RNA as input material and involves just three seamless steps (reverse transcription, tagmentation and strand extension and PCR), without the need for a second strand synthesis step.
evidence: Described in the methods and shown in Figure 2a

claim: TRACE-seq involves just three seamless steps: reverse transcription, tagmentation and strand extension and PCR.
source: With the help of TRACE-seq, these steps are replaced with a 'one-tube' protocol (Figure 2a), which uses total RNA as input material and involves just three seamless steps (reverse transcription, tagmentation and strand extension and PCR), without the need for a second strand synthesis step.
evidence: Described in the methods and shown in Figure 2a

claim: TRACE-seq does not need a second strand synthesis step.
source: With the help of TRACE-seq, these steps are replaced with a 'one-tube' protocol (Figure 2a), which uses total RNA as input material and involves just three seamless steps (reverse transcription, tagmentation and strand extension and PCR), without the need for a second strand synthesis step.
evidence: Described in the methods and shown in Figure 2a

claim: TRACE-seq with 200 ng total RNA as input is highly reproducible among three replicates.
source: We first conducted TRACE-seq with 200 ng total RNA as input and tested several enzymes and conditions (Supplementary file 1); we observed very high correlation in gene-expression levels among three replicates, indicating TRACE-seq is highly reproducible (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by correlation data shown in Figure 2b

claim: TRACE-seq results are highly reproducible among replicates with 20 ng and 2 ng total RNA input.
source: To test the robustness of TRACE-seq, we performed the experiments with 20 ng and 2 ng total RNA. TRACE-seq results are again highly reproducible among replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by correlation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b

claim: Gene expression levels measured using different amounts of starting materials remain consistent with each other in TRACE-seq.
source: More importantly, gene expression levels measured using different amount of starting materials remain consistent with each other (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by correlation data shown in Figure 2c

claim: 97% of genes detected by TRACE-seq overlap with NEBNext library.
source: Overall, in spite of gene body coverage bias, TRACE-seq allows construction of high complexity RNA libraries and demonstrates similar performance as traditional RNA library preparation methods in terms of detected genes (97% and 93% overlapped with NEBNext and Smart-seq2 library respectively), gene expression measurement (R > 0.90) and differential expression analysis (R > 0.99), but outcompetes the traditional methods in terms of speed, convenience and cost.
evidence: Calculated from comparison data presented in the manuscript

claim: 93% of genes detected by TRACE-seq overlap with Smart-seq2 library.
source: Overall, in spite of gene body coverage bias, TRACE-seq allows construction of high complexity RNA libraries and demonstrates similar performance as traditional RNA library preparation methods in terms of detected genes (97% and 93% overlapped with NEBNext and Smart-seq2 library respectively), gene expression measurement (R > 0.90) and differential expression analysis (R > 0.99), but outcompetes the traditional methods in terms of speed, convenience and cost.
evidence: Calculated from comparison data presented in the manuscript

claim: TRACE-seq shows comparable performance to traditional methods in gene expression measurement (R > 0.90).
source: Overall, in spite of gene body coverage bias, TRACE-seq allows construction of high complexity RNA libraries and demonstrates similar performance as traditional RNA library preparation methods in terms of detected genes (97% and 93% overlapped with NEBNext and Smart-seq2 library respectively), gene expression measurement (R > 0.90) and differential expression analysis (R > 0.99), but outcompetes the traditional methods in terms of speed, convenience and cost.
evidence: Supported by correlation data presented in the manuscript

claim: TRACE-seq shows comparable performance to traditional methods in differential expression analysis (R > 0.99).
source: Overall, in spite of gene body coverage bias, TRACE-seq allows construction of high complexity RNA libraries and demonstrates similar performance as traditional RNA library preparation methods in terms of detected genes (97% and 93% overlapped with NEBNext and Smart-seq2 library respectively), gene expression measurement (R > 0.90) and differential expression analysis (R > 0.99), but outcompetes the traditional methods in terms of speed, convenience and cost.
evidence: Supported by correlation data shown in Figure 3c

claim: TRACE-seq showed a higher rRNA contamination (~9%) when total RNA was used as input.
source: We found that TRACE-seq libraries exhibited similar percentage of reads mapped to annotated transcripts, rRNA contamination and gene numbers to NEBNext data when mRNA was used as input, but a higher rRNA contamination when total RNA was used as input (~9%, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 2

claim: A similar percentage of rRNA contamination was observed in Smart-seq2 libraries.
source: In addition, a similar percentage of rRNA contamination was also observed in Smart-seq2 libraries (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 3

claim: The insert size of TRACE-seq library was moderately shorter than traditional methods.
source: The insert size of TRACE-seq library was moderately shorter (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d); in the meanwhile, TRACE-seq shows a higher coefficient of variation of gene coverage (0.54–0.70 vs 0.42–0.44, Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d

claim: TRACE-seq shows a higher coefficient of variation of gene coverage (0.54–0.70 vs 0.42–0.44) compared to traditional methods.
source: The insert size of TRACE-seq library was moderately shorter (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d); in the meanwhile, TRACE-seq shows a higher coefficient of variation of gene coverage (0.54–0.70 vs 0.42–0.44, Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e

claim: TRACE-seq showed a slight tendency to 3' end of the gene body.
source: We further found that TRACE-seq showed a slight tendency to 3' end of the gene body (Figure 2f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by gene body coverage data shown in Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1f

claim: For transcripts shorter than 1 kb, TRACE-seq shows comparable gene body coverage to NEBNext kit and Smart-seq2 libraries.
source: When transcripts were grouped according to annotated lengths, we found comparable gene body coverage for transcripts shorter than 1 kb among TRACE-seq, NEBNext kit and Smart-seq2 libraries.
evidence: Supported by gene body coverage analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f

claim: For transcripts with length between 1 and 4 kb, a slight 3' end bias was observed in TRACE-seq library.
source: For transcripts with length between 1 and 4 kb, a slight 3' end bias was observed in TRACE-seq library, while for transcripts longer than 4 kb, the central regions of transcripts were less covered by both TRACE-seq and Smart-seq2.
evidence: Supported by gene body coverage analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f

claim: For transcripts longer than 4 kb, the central regions of transcripts were less covered by both TRACE-seq and Smart-seq2.
source: For transcripts with length between 1 and 4 kb, a slight 3' end bias was observed in TRACE-seq library, while for transcripts longer than 4 kb, the central regions of transcripts were less covered by both TRACE-seq and Smart-seq2.
evidence: Supported by gene body coverage analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f

claim: Using rRNA depletion together with random-primed cDNA synthesis solved the 3' end bias but introduced a 5' end bias.
source: We also performed TRACE-seq by using rRNA depletion together with random-primed cDNA synthesis. While this solved the 3' end bias, a 5' end bias appeared, which is a common phenomenon when using random primers during reverse transcription (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by gene body coverage data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f

claim: 5' end bias is a common phenomenon when using random primers during reverse transcription.
source: We also performed TRACE-seq by using rRNA depletion together with random-primed cDNA synthesis. While this solved the 3' end bias, a 5' end bias appeared, which is a common phenomenon when using random primers during reverse transcription (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: GC content is unnoticeably affected by the gene body coverage bias in TRACE-seq.
source: In spite of the gene body coverage bias, GC content (Figure 2g) and library complexity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g) are unnoticeably affected.
evidence: Supported by GC content analysis shown in Figure 2g

claim: Library complexity is unnoticeably affected by the gene body coverage bias in TRACE-seq.
source: In spite of the gene body coverage bias, GC content (Figure 2g) and library complexity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g) are unnoticeably affected.
evidence: Supported by library complexity analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g

claim: Gene expression measurement is unaffected by gene body coverage bias when using RNA with high quality (RIN: 9.5).
source: In addition, the gene expression measurement (Figure 2e) is also unaffected here because of the use of RNA with high quality (RIN: 9.5, Figure 2—figure supplement 1h); yet, cautions might be taken when the quality of RNA is compromised.
evidence: Supported by gene expression correlation data and RIN assessment

claim: TRACE-seq detected 4577 differentially expressed genes (3264 up-regulated genes and 1313 down-regulated genes) between undifferentiated and differentiated mESCs.
source: As shown in Figure 3a, TRACE-seq successfully detected 4577 differentially expressed genes (3264 up-regulated genes and 1313 down-regulated genes), while NEBNext detected 4452 differentially expressed genes (3157 up-regulated genes and 1295 down-regulated genes).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3a

claim: NEBNext detected 4452 differentially expressed genes (3157 up-regulated genes and 1295 down-regulated genes) between undifferentiated and differentiated mESCs.
source: As shown in Figure 3a, TRACE-seq successfully detected 4577 differentially expressed genes (3264 up-regulated genes and 1313 down-regulated genes), while NEBNext detected 4452 differentially expressed genes (3157 up-regulated genes and 1295 down-regulated genes).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3a

claim: The overlapping gene number between TRACE-seq and NEBNext for differentially expressed genes is 4,071.
source: The overlapping gene number is 4,071, showing very high consistency between methods (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram shown in Figure 3b

claim: The fold change of the 4071 overlapping genes is highly correlated between TRACE-seq and NEBNext (R > 0.99).
source: Besides, the fold change of the 4071 overlapping genes is highly correlated between the two methods (R > 0.99, Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3c

claim: TRACE-seq shows excellent performance in differential gene expression analysis.
source: Therefore, TRACE-seq shows excellent performance in differential gene expression analysis.
evidence: Inferred from the high overlap and correlation of differentially expressed genes

claim: Tn5 exhibits a slight insertion bias on dsDNA substrates.
source: Previous studies found that Tn5 exhibits a slight insertion bias on dsDNA substrates (Goryshin et al., 1998; Green et al., 2012; Lodge et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: An apparent insertion signature on RNA/DNA hybrids was observed for Tn5.
source: Similar to dsDNA substrates, we also observed an apparent insertion signature on RNA/DNA hybrids (Figure 2—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Supported by nucleotide composition analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1i

claim: Per-position information contents of Tn5 insertion sites on RNA/DNA hybrids were extremely low.
source: Nevertheless, per-position information contents were extremely low, suggesting such insertion bias is less likely to affect gene body coverage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: Supported by WebLogo analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1j

claim: The insertion bias of Tn5 on RNA/DNA hybrids is less likely to affect gene body coverage.
source: Nevertheless, per-position information contents were extremely low, suggesting such insertion bias is less likely to affect gene body coverage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1j).

claim: TRACE-seq outcompetes traditional methods in terms of speed, convenience and cost.

claim: An engineered, hyperactive Tn5 transposase from E. coli can bind to synthetic 19 bp mosaic end-recognition sequences appended to Illumina sequencing adapters.
source: Taking advantage of this catalytic activity, transposases are widely used in many biomedical applications: for instance, an engineered, hyperactive Tn5 transposase from E. coli can bind to synthetic 19 bp mosaic end-recognition sequences appended to Illumina sequencing adapters (termed 'Tn5 transposome') (Adey et al., 2010) and has been utilized in an in vitro double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) tagmentation reaction (namely simultaneously fragment and tag a target sequence with sequencing adaptors) to achieve rapid and low-input library construction for next-generation sequencing (Adey et al., 2010; Goryshin and Reznikoff, 1998; Picelli et al., 2014a; Caruccio, 2011; Ramsköld et al., 2012; Gertz et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adey et al., 2010
